lesson.title: They're All the Same to Us: Out-Group Homogeneity Bias
lesson.summary: Out-group homogeneity bias is the tendency to perceive members of an out-group as more similar to one another than members of one's own in-group, even when the actual diversity within both groups is comparable.
lesson.body:
Out-group homogeneity bias is closely related to, but distinct from, the in-group bias just discussed. In-group bias is about evaluation, giving our own group more favorable treatment. Out-group homogeneity bias is about perception, specifically the perception of variability. People consistently judge the members of a group they do not belong to as more alike in personality, attitudes, and behavior than the members of their own group, who are seen as diverse individuals. The common shorthand for this is the sense that "they are all alike, but we are all different."

This bias also connects back to stereotypes. A stereotype is a simplified belief applied to an entire group, and out-group homogeneity bias helps explain why stereotypes about out-groups feel so easy to form and so resistant to exceptions. If a group is perceived as fundamentally uniform, then a single trait, whether accurate or not, can seem to describe the whole group reasonably well. By contrast, because we perceive far more internal variation within our own group, a stereotype about "us" tends to feel obviously wrong, since we can immediately think of many people in our own group who do not fit it.

Part of the explanation is simple exposure. Most people have much more contact with, and much more differentiated knowledge about, their own group's subtypes than an out-group's. A person deeply embedded in their own profession, campus, or community naturally learns about its internal factions and personality types, while an outsider only sees a single undifferentiated category from a distance. This same logic has been used to help explain the well documented difficulty many people have in distinguishing individual faces of unfamiliar racial or ethnic out-groups compared to their own, sometimes called the cross race effect or own race bias in face recognition research, a pattern with real consequences in contexts like eyewitness identification.

The upshot is that in-group bias and out-group homogeneity bias tend to reinforce each other. Favoring our own group encourages us to pay closer attention to its internal richness, while giving less attention to the out-group flattens it into a caricature, which in turn makes it easier to treat out-group members as interchangeable rather than as individuals. Together, these two biases form a significant part of the psychological foundation for intergroup prejudice and discrimination.
